transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, I don't see an option that increases our bay capacity or staffing beyond what's been laid out. But I want to be explicit about the clinical risk from my side as the pediatric emergency physician. Two RNs and one RT covering six simultaneously occupied monitored-observation bays means each RN is responsible for three monitored patients. For pediatric respiratory illness patients who may need continuous oxygen titration, aerosolized treatments, and frequent reassessment, that is a demanding ratio — not impossible, but it leaves no room for a deteriorating patient who requires one-on-one attention. If one child decompensates during the surge window, that RN is pulled away from their other two patients, and the remaining RN is suddenly covering five. I agree we need to formally acknowledge this is a zero-margin plan. My recommendation is that we document two contingencies explicitly in the operating plan: first, a diversion or transfer protocol for a seventh monitored-observation patient since the main ED cannot hold that overflow per our surge plan; and second, an early-warning trigger — if even one oxygen outlet fails overnight or if any patient in the observation wing requires escalation to one-on-one nursing, we activate that diversion protocol immediately rather than waiting for a seventh arrival. I'd rather over-prepare than find ourselves unable to safely care for the six patients we've already forecasted.
